traveler: San Vito (Vitus of Lucania, Sankt Veit, Svaty Vit, Sveti Vid)
title: The Boy Carried Out of Rome: a Sicilian Legend, a Scattered Body, and a Feast Day That Kept Colliding With Europe
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mazara del Vallo, the birth in the senator's house
stops.date_confidence: traditional only; the sources give the reign of Diocletian and no year, and the year 290 is a conventional placement
stops.campa: On the southwestern coast of Sicily, in the town the Romans call Mazara, a son is born to the senator Hylas, who keeps the old gods and the old offices under Diocletian. The child is named Vito. The house he is born in will become a church, and the city will still be calling it the house of San Vito sixteen centuries later. Nothing in the record fixes the year. The passio that tells the story is written four hundred years after the fact and gives a reign rather than a date. Mazara keeps him anyway, as a native son who left and became a saint elsewhere.
suggested_refs: The Chiesa di San Vito in Urbe at Mazara del Vallo, built on the traditional birth house

stops.name: Mazara del Vallo, the nurse and the tutor
stops.date_confidence: legendary; no source dates the baptism, and both companions are called probably fictitious by modern scholarship
stops.campa: The senator's household includes a nurse, Crescentia, and her husband Modestus, who is set over the boy as tutor. Both are Christians, and they baptize him without telling his father. The Roman Breviary states it as one flat line in the lessons for the fifteenth of June and states nothing else about how a pagan magistrate came to hand his son to two believers. Modern scholarship holds both of them probably fictitious, invented to give a child martyr the adults a child would need. The legend requires them. The record does not have them.
stops.quote: Vitus while yet a child was baptized, unknown to his father.
stops.quote_source: Roman Breviary, Matins lessons for 15 June, in Dom Prosper Gueranger, The Liturgical Year, tr. Laurence Shepherd
suggested_refs: The Matins lessons for 15 June in the pre-1969 Roman Breviary, naming all three martyrs

stops.name: Mazara del Vallo, harps and pipes against a child
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the hagiography splits on whether he is seven or twelve at this point and no source reached reconciles the two
stops.campa: The senator learns what his household has done and answers it first with pleasure rather than force. He fills the rooms with harps and pipes and every instrument he can find, brings in girls to play with the boy, and arranges all the delights available to a man of his rank, to soften him and change his heart. Caxton renders the whole attempt in one long sentence in 1483. It fails. What follows is a beating, and then the tutor and the nurse take the boy out of the house.
stops.quote: made come to him harps, pipes and all manner instruments that he might have, and after did do come maidens for to play with him, and made him to have all manner of delights that he might get, to mollify and change his heart.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), The Life of Saint Vitus
suggested_refs: Caxton's 1483 Golden Legend, the life of Saint Vitus, at christianiconography.info

stops.name: San Vito Lo Capo, the landing on the cape
stops.date_confidence: local tradition only; no text older than the town's own memory places the fugitives here, and the town is named after him
stops.campa: On the cape at Sicily's northwestern tip, local memory puts the three fugitives ashore before their crossing. No source older than the town's own tradition places them here. Every fifteenth of June three performers come in by boat at sunset as Vito, Crescenzia and Modesto, and the beach receives them again. The sanctuary above the strand is later built as a fortress, its walls thick enough to hold off the corsair raids that come in from the same water the three are said to have crossed.
suggested_refs: The fortified sanctuary of San Vito Lo Capo, built against corsair raids

stops.name: The open sea off Sicily, the boat to Lucania
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the passio gives no port, no vessel and no season. Pin inherited byte-identical from giles.journey.json
stops.campa: The three take ship for the mainland. This is the same water Giles will cross going the other way, west toward Provence, three and a half centuries on, and the atlas keeps one pin for both passages. The legend supplies no port and no vessel, only the fact of a crossing from Sicily to Lucania, which in this period names a stretch of country covering parts of what are now Basilicata and Campania. Everything specific about the voyage belongs to the towns that wanted it rather than to the text.
stops.quote: Vitus, being warned by an angel, fled to another country, in company with Modestus and Crescentia, who had brought him up.
stops.quote_source: Roman Breviary, Matins lessons for 15 June, in Gueranger, The Liturgical Year, tr. Shepherd; Bute's translation renders the same lesson as fled out of the country, in company with his foster-parents
suggested_refs: giles.journey.json, the open sea off Sicily, the storm calmed: the same pin, the opposite direction

stops.name: Piana del Sele, the years of miracles
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the years in Lucania are undated in every source reached
stops.campa: Beside the river Sele the three settle and are left alone for years. Vito grows up in the plain and heals people in it, and the country fills with the report of him long before Rome has any reason to hear the name. The Roman Martyrology, keeping the older river name, still says near the river Silaro. This is the Lucanian version of the life, in which Sicily is only the beginning and the plain is where everything that matters happens, and it is the version the liturgical books of the Latin church adopted.
suggested_refs: The plain of the Sele in ancient Lucania, the setting of the Roman Martyrology entry for 15 June
sources: Vatican News, San Vito, martire in Lucania

stops.name: The Sele valley, the preside Valeriano
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the seventh-century passio names the official and gives no year
stops.campa: The provincial governor, whom the passio names Valeriano, has the boy arrested for his faith and for the following it has gathered. He is questioned, imprisoned, and, in the telling, released by an angel who opens the cell. The Golden Legend has him answer the governor's threats with an offer to cure him instead. The pattern set here holds for the rest of the story: the authorities apply an ordeal, the ordeal does not work, and the failure of the ordeal is the miracle. Italian sources call the man preside, a praeses, not a prefect.
stops.quote: I may well heal thee in the name of my Lord Jesu Christ.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), Vitus to the provost Valerian
suggested_refs: The seventh-century Passio Sancti Viti, BHL 8711, naming il preside Valeriano

stops.name: Rome, the palace, the possessed boy
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the Roman episode is undated in the sources and is placed here inside the traditional martyrdom year
stops.campa: The emperor's son is possessed, and the spirit in him announces that it will not leave until the child from Lucania is brought. Vito is fetched to Rome and the spirit goes out. Diocletian, who has just watched a boy do what his own priests could not, offers the ordinary settlement of the persecution: sacrifice to the gods and live. Caxton's text confuses the possessed son with his father and calls the boy Diocletian, and corrupts Lucania into Lucca. The confusion stands in the quote because the quote is the source's own wording.
stops.quote: Diocletian, son of the emperor, had a wicked spirit in his body, and said openly that he would not go out till the child of Lucca named Vitus was come.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), The Life of Saint Vitus
suggested_refs: The exorcism of the emperor's son in the Golden Legend cycle of Saint Vitus

stops.name: Rome, the cauldron and the lions
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the arena is popular devotion, not attestation, and no ancient source ties the Colosseum to Vito by name
stops.campa: Refusal is read as sorcery and the machinery starts. The three are put into a cauldron of boiling pitch, or molten lead depending on the telling, and come out unmarked. They are thrown to lions, and the lions lie down. Popular devotion moves the beasts to the Colosseum, though historians dispute that the building staged Christian executions at all and nothing ancient names it for Vito. The cauldron stays with him permanently. It is what he holds in the paintings, the way Catherine of Alexandria holds her wheel.
stops.quote: My child, take counsel in thy works and do sacrifice unto our gods to the end that thou die not an evil death.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), Diocletian to Vitus after the exorcism
suggested_refs: The cauldron, rooster, lion and martyr's palm of Vitus iconography
catherine_alexandria.journey.json, the wheel as the same kind of attribute

stops.name: Rome, the gibbet and the angel
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the deliverance and the flight back to Lucania are the passio's own account and are attested nowhere else
stops.campa: Last comes the gibbet, the three of them hung up together, the nurse who has followed the boy since Mazara hanging beside him. Then an earthquake takes down the temples, the emperor says the line the legend exists to record, and an angel lifts the three out of Rome and sets them down again in Lucania. They are not executed. Rome runs out of ways to kill them, and they leave. What kills them is the accumulated damage, days later, in the plain by the river where they had been left alone for years.
stops.quote: Alas! alas! a child hath overcome me.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), Diocletian after the earthquake and the destruction of the temples
suggested_refs: The angelic deliverance and return flight, the structural hinge of the Passio Sancti Viti

stops.name: Piana del Sele, the three die together
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Italian tradition gives 303 and the day is fixed by liturgical use rather than by any record
stops.campa: They die beside the Sele, worn out by what Rome did to them, on the fifteenth of June, in the year the Italian tradition gives as 303. The date will outlast every other detail of the story. It is the day the Latin church keeps, the day German dancers converge on eleven centuries later, and the day, by the Julian reckoning, on which a Serbian army loses a battle that reorganizes a nation's memory of itself. None of that is in the passio. The passio has three exhausted bodies in a river plain.
stops.quote: In Basilicata, near the river Silaro, the birthday of the holy martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, who were brought thither from Sicily, in the reign of Diocletian, and after being plunged into a vessel of melted lead, after being exposed to the beasts, and on the pillory, from which torments they escaped uninjured through the power of God, they ended their religious combats.
stops.quote_source: Roman Martyrology (Martyrologium Romanum), entry for 15 June, English translation
suggested_refs: The Roman Martyrology entry for 15 June, which keeps Lucania and drops Rome entirely
sources: Vatican News, San Vito, martire in Lucania

stops.name: Marigliano, the rival grave
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: Cathopedia puts the burial at Marianus, identified with Marigliano, against the Sele-valley tradition forty kilometres away
stops.campa: A matron gathers the bodies, embalms them with spices, and buries them. The Roman Breviary calls her Florentia and names no place. Cathopedia carries a strand in which she is Fiorenza and the burial is not by the Sele at all but at a site called Marianus, identified with Marigliano east of Naples, where a church of San Vito stands over an early medieval martyrial basilica. Forty kilometres separate the two graves and no source reached reconciles them. Both towns keep him. Only one of them can be right.
stops.quote: Their remains were gathered up by a noble lady named Florentia who, embalming them with spices, honorably buried them.
stops.quote_source: Roman Breviary, Matins lessons for 15 June, in Gueranger, The Liturgical Year, tr. Shepherd
suggested_refs: The chiesa di San Vito at Marigliano, built over an early medieval martyrial basilica

stops.name: Rome, the shrine Gelasius mentions
stops.date_confidence: attested to the pontificate of Gelasius I, 492-496, but not to a year; the shrine's location is named by no source reached
stops.campa: Two centuries after the traditional date of the deaths, a pope writing between 492 and 496 mentions a shrine of Vitus in Rome. That is the whole of it. A shrine exists, in the city where the legend has him tortured, and Gelasius has occasion to name it in correspondence. Where it stood is recorded in nothing reached for this journey. The cult is older than any surviving account of the man. The veneration comes first here, and the biography is written afterward to explain it.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Pope Gelasius I, 492-496, earliest Roman notice of a shrine of Vitus

stops.name: Auxerre, the name enters the martyrology
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the Hieronymianum was compiled in northern Italy in the 430s-440s, but the surviving text carrying these entries is a Gallic reworking of c. 600 and the oldest manuscripts are eighth century
stops.campa: The oldest written notice of Vitus is a line in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, four words and three names, placing them in Sicily. The compilation was made in northern Italy around the 430s, but the text that survives, the one that actually carries these entries, is a reworking done in Gaul, probably here at Auxerre, around the year 600, and the oldest manuscripts of it are eighth century. A cult routinely dated to 450 is documented, in what physically exists, a hundred and fifty years later, and the two figures are not the same claim.
stops.quote: In Sicilia, Viti, Modesti et Crescentiae
stops.quote_source: Martyrologium Hieronymianum, quoted secondhand in the Catholic Encyclopedia article on Sts. Vitus, Modestus and Crescentia; not seen in a critical edition
suggested_refs: The Gallic recension of the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, probably Auxerre, c. 600
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, Sts. Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia

stops.name: Pavia, the church of San Marino
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: the Italian tradition gives 755, Aistulf and Pavia; English-language sources give 756, Fulrad and Saint-Denis
stops.campa: The Lombard king Aistulf brings relics of Vitus to Pavia, to the church of San Marino, which he founded and in which he will be buried. That is the Italian account and it gives 755. The Frankish account gives 756, a different agent, and a different destination, and neither acknowledges the other. From this point the saint is an object that kings move. Aistulf takes him for a church he built to be buried in, and the shrines that hold him can be persuaded to let him go again.
suggested_refs: The church of San Marino at Pavia, founded by Aistulf, who was buried in it

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the abbot's translation
stops.date_confidence: attested in English-language tradition to 756 and Abbot Fulrad; irreconcilable with the Pavia account of 755
stops.campa: Abbot Fulrad brings relics of Vitus north to the royal abbey of Saint-Denis, one shipment inside the traffic that furnishes Frankish churches with Roman bones. The year given is 756, one year after Pavia, and the sources that give each do not acknowledge the other. Saint-Denis will hold him eighty years, the shortest tenancy in the chain, and will then give him away for reasons of state rather than lose him. It sends him east, into country Charlemagne conquered a generation earlier, and the northern half of the cult starts there.
suggested_refs: The abbey of Saint-Denis and the eighth-century traffic in Roman relics

stops.name: Corvey Abbey, the Saxon patron
stops.date_confidence: attested to 836; the coordinates given in the research pool were wrong by up to two kilometres and are corrected here
stops.campa: Saint-Denis passes the relics on to the new Benedictine house at Corvey on the Weser, founded to hold Saxony for the church after Charlemagne's wars there. The gift remakes the abbey. Vitus becomes patron of the Saxons, pilgrims start arriving, and Corvey grows into one of the richest monasteries in central Europe on the strength of him. The chapels and the feast dances that will later carry his name across Germany run downstream from this transfer of a Sicilian boy's bones into Westphalia.
suggested_refs: The Carolingian westwork of Corvey Abbey, raised on the wealth the relics brought

stops.name: Prague Castle, the arm bone and the rotunda
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: 925 is given for Henry I's gift of the relic and 930 for the founding of the rotunda, and the two dates are not reconciled across sources
stops.campa: Henry the Fowler gives Duke Wenceslaus a hand bone of Vitus out of the northern stock, and Wenceslaus builds a rotunda on the castle hill to house it. The sources give 925 for the gift and 930 for the foundation and leave the difference standing. The relic arrives before the building, and the building is named for the relic, so the principal church of Bohemia carries the name of a Sicilian child before it is a cathedral, and before there is a kingdom for it to crown.
suggested_refs: The Romanesque rotunda of St Vitus at Prague Castle, founded by Wenceslaus

segments.name: The Cathedral That Keeps His Name

stops.name: Prague Castle, the basilica of Spytihnev
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1060
stops.campa: The rotunda is too small for the traffic it has generated. Prince Spytihnev the Second pulls it down and raises a Romanesque basilica on the same ground, keeping the dedication. The saint whose legend has him carried out of Rome by an angel is now the fixed point of a dynasty's building program, and each rebuilding will be larger than the last. Nothing about Vitus requires this. A hand bone arrived, and the state kept enlarging the house around it for nine hundred years.
suggested_refs: The Romanesque basilica of Spytihnev II, second church on the St Vitus site

stops.name: Prague Castle, the foundation stone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: King John of Bohemia lays the foundation stone of the Gothic cathedral on the twenty first of November, in the same season Prague is raised to an archbishopric. Matthias of Arras designs it. Charles the Fourth wants it as coronation church of the Bohemian kings, as crypt for his dynasty, and as the reliquary of the kingdom's most valuable bones. The dedication to a Sicilian child martyr whom nobody in Prague could place on a map is inherited, and is never questioned.
suggested_refs: The 1344 elevation of Prague to an archbishopric, coinciding with the cathedral's foundation

stops.name: Prague Castle, the relics come up from Pavia
stops.date_confidence: thinly sourced: widely repeated, but no source reached documents the transfer independently of later retellings
stops.campa: Charles the Fourth brings relics of Vitus from Pavia to Prague, adding to the hand bone that has been on the hill since Wenceslaus. Pavia has held them, by the Italian account, since Aistulf put them in San Marino six hundred years earlier. No source reached documents the transfer independently of later retellings, and the emperor who orders it is the same man who commissioned the building they are going into, which is a standing reason to want the account to be true.
suggested_refs: The 1355 translation from Pavia, the last major addition to the Prague relics

stops.name: Prague Castle, Parler takes the site
stops.date_confidence: attested: Parler arrives 1356 and dies 13 July 1399; the frequently printed span 1352-1397 is wrong at both ends and erases the gap after Matthias of Arras
stops.campa: Matthias of Arras has been dead four years when Peter Parler arrives from Swabia, twenty three years old, and takes over the site. He runs it until his death on the thirteenth of July 1399, forty three years, and in that time the cathedral acquires the vaulting and the portrait busts that make it his rather than his predecessor's. The four year gap after Matthias is real and is usually closed without comment; the dates 1352 to 1397, printed everywhere, are wrong at both ends.
suggested_refs: Peter Parler's triforium portrait busts in St Vitus Cathedral, including his own

stops.name: Prague Castle, the consecration
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The cathedral is consecrated on the twelfth of May, timed to the millennium of Wenceslaus, who founded the rotunda that stood on this ground. Construction has run just short of six hundred years. In 1997 the dedication will be widened to name Wenceslaus and Adalbert beside Vitus, for the millennium of Adalbert's death, so the saint who arrived as a hand bone in a Saxon gift ends by sharing his own building with two Bohemians. He keeps first place in the name. The country calls it Svaty Vit.
suggested_refs: The 1929 consecration and the 1997 widening of the dedication to Wenceslaus and Adalbert

segments.name: The Dance That Takes His Name

stops.name: Maastricht, the bridge that went into the Meuse
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved: the dancing-mania literature gives 1278 and dancers, Maastricht's own record gives 1275 and a procession. The bridge that fell no longer exists; the pin is approximate, south of the surviving Sint Servaasbrug
stops.campa: Two hundred people dancing on a bridge over the Meuse bring it down, and the survivors are carried to a chapel of Saint Vitus nearby and healed. That is the dancing mania literature, dating it 1278. Maastricht's own record dates a bridge collapse to 1275, blames the weight of a religious procession, and counts four hundred dead. Cause and year both differ and neither account yields. The bridge itself is gone. The one standing today was built afterward, slightly to the north, and paid for with indulgences.
suggested_refs: The old Roman bridge at Maastricht, replaced by the indulgence-funded Sint Servaasbrug

stops.name: Aachen, the dancers of midsummer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty fourth of June the dancing breaks out in Aachen and runs outward through the Rhineland and the Low Countries within weeks. People dance in the streets until they collapse, and the chroniclers reach for Saint Vitus to name what is happening, though his feast passed nine days earlier. The association is already automatic by 1374. Processions of dancers end at his chapels, the outbreaks cluster near the fifteenth of June, and the sufferers pray to the saint whose name the affliction has taken.
suggested_refs: The 1374 Rhineland outbreak, the first well-recorded dancing mania

stops.name: Schaffhausen, the monk who danced to death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the research pool paired this with Ulm, which appears in no source, and pinned it in open country near Bad Waldsee. Both the pairing and the pin are discarded
stops.campa: A monk at Schaffhausen dances until it kills him, and in the same year women at Zurich are seized by the same frenzy. Outbreaks like these recur through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries across the German and French speaking towns, each folded back into one explanatory frame: a curse from Saint Vitus, or a summons from him. The distinction between curse and summons is never settled by anyone at the time, and the treatment for both is the same, which is to take the dancers to his chapel.
suggested_refs: The 1428 Schaffhausen and Zurich episodes in the dancing-mania record

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, among the Fourteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional; pin and date inherited byte-identical from saint_barbara.journey.json. Flagged: giles.journey.json carries the same shrine at 50.1156, 11.0544 dated 1446-07-28, and the two existing files are not reconciled
stops.campa: Above the Cistercian abbey of Langheim the shepherd Hermann Leicht sees a child in the field, and then fourteen of them, asking a chapel. The Fourteen Holy Helpers become a fixed devotional set and a basilica rises on the meadow between 1743 and 1772. Vitus stands among the fourteen by tradition, beside Barbara, who has been in Regensburg's prayers for a century, and Giles, the only one of them who was not a martyr. The atlas keeps one pin here for all of them and this journey inherits it unchanged.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, Vierzehnheiligen, Bad Staffelstein
saint_barbara.journey.json and giles.journey.json, the same shrine, two slightly different pins

stops.name: Strasbourg, the woman in the street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the name Frau Troffea is not in the cited sources and comes from John Waller's popular account, so this stop leaves her unnamed
stops.campa: In July a woman begins dancing alone in a Strasbourg street and does not stop. Within a month between fifty and four hundred people are dancing with her, and several are reported to have died of exhaustion. It is the best documented episode of the whole phenomenon and the one that fixes the saint's name to it in popular memory. The name usually given to the first dancer comes from a modern retelling rather than from the record. Strasbourg in 1518 is a free imperial city, not French for another hundred and sixty three years.
suggested_refs: The 1518 Strasbourg dancing plague, the best-documented outbreak of the sequence

stops.name: Ingolstadt, the Wednesday after his feast
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; pin inherited byte-identical from johann_faust.journey.json, whose council minute dates the expulsion by the feast of Saint Vitus
stops.campa: The city council orders a man calling himself Doctor Jorg Faustus of Heidelberg to spend his pennies somewhere else, and dates the order the only way a German town dates anything: the Wednesday after the feast of Saint Vitus, the seventeenth of June. This is the single place in the corpus where the saint's name turns up in a document about somebody else's life, and it is there as a date rather than as devotion. Nobody in the room is venerating him. The clerk needs a fixed point in June and reaches for the feast.
suggested_refs: The Ingolstadt council minute of 17 June 1528, dated by the feast of Saint Vitus
johann_faust.journey.json, the same pin and the same day

stops.name: Drefelhausen, the women who come back every year
stops.date_confidence: seventeenth century, no closer date in the sources; the research pool placed Drefelhausen in Bavaria, sixty kilometres from the actual site in Wurttemberg near Weissenstein, and the pin is corrected
stops.campa: At a chapel of Saint Vitus in Wurttemberg, near Weissenstein in the territory of Ulm, women come once a year to dance. The physician Gregor Horst watches and writes it down. They dance all day and all night, and one of them tells him she has done this every year for twenty years, another for thirty two. The dancing is annual and expected, an appointment kept with the saint, and the church that receives them is the one whose mass asks that his intercession benefit bodies as well as souls.
stops.quote: We, who have been filled with Thy solemn blessing, ask, O Lord, that, through the intercession of Thy holy Martyrs Vitus, Modestus and Crescentia, this healing sacrament may benefit both our bodies and our souls.
stops.quote_source: Missale Romanum, Postcommunion for the Mass of Sts. Vitus, Modestus and Crescentia, 15 June
suggested_refs: Gregor Horst's account of the annual dancing at the Vitus chapel of Drefelhausen

stops.name: London, the physician names the chorea
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1686 is the conventional figure for Sydenham's description and is confirmed by no source reached; only the naming convention is attested
stops.campa: An English physician describes a chorea of children, the involuntary jerking that medicine will call Sydenham's chorea after him. The older folk name attaches itself and will not come off: Saint Vitus's Dance, carried into clinical English out of German villages where people danced before his statue on his feast. The date usually printed for the description is confirmed by nothing reached here. The saint is now the eponym of a neurological disorder, and in English the folk name and the clinical name run side by side from here on.
suggested_refs: Thomas Sydenham's description of childhood chorea, source of the modern clinical name

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the Anna-Kapelle
stops.date_confidence: inferred, following catherine_alexandria.journey.json; pin inherited byte-identical rather than duplicated
stops.campa: In a small chapel on the Main a carved Nothelferaltar sets the Fourteen Holy Helpers in a row, and a plaque carries the rhyme that names the three virgin martyrs among them by their instruments: Margaretha with the worm, Barbara with the tower, Katharina with the wheel. Vitus stands in the same rank holding his cauldron. The atlas already pins this altar for Catherine of Alexandria, and the pin is inherited here rather than duplicated for a saint who shares the frame.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: Traditional Rhineland mnemonic rhyme, inscribed on the plaque at the Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main
suggested_refs: The Nothelferaltar of the Anna-Kapelle at Obernburg am Main
catherine_alexandria.journey.json and saint_barbara.journey.json, the same plaque pin

stops.name: Gazimestan, the battle on his feast
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, Julian; the pin is the monument, which stands five to seven kilometres from the presumed battlefield, and the research pool's coordinates were wrong by about six kilometres
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of June by the Julian calendar, the feast of Saint Vitus, an Ottoman army under Murad the First meets a Serbian led coalition under Prince Lazar on the field of Kosovo. Both commanders die in the fighting. The defeat becomes the founding wound of Serbian national memory, and the saint's day becomes Vidovdan, the day of Vid, kept for Lazar and for the martyrs of the field. The pin marks the monument. The fighting is presumed to have been some kilometres from it.
suggested_refs: The Gazimestan monument on the Kosovo field, marking the battle of 1389

stops.name: Belgrade, war declared on Vidovdan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Serbia declares war on the Ottoman Empire on Vidovdan, having chosen the date. The feast of a Sicilian child martyr, carried into the Slavic calendar through Corvey and Prague, is now an instrument of state timing, and later governments keep reaching for it. The enemy named in the declaration is the same empire whose army won on the field in 1389. Four hundred and eighty seven years after Kosovo, the commemoration of a defeat is being used to announce that the defeat is going to be answered.
suggested_refs: The Serbian declaration of war of 15 June 1876, timed to Vidovdan

stops.name: Belgrade, the alliance signed the day after
stops.date_confidence: corrected: 16 June Julian is the day AFTER Vidovdan, which falls on 15 June Julian. The research pool claimed the signing coincided with the feast; the cited source explicitly denies it
stops.campa: The Austro-Serbian Alliance is signed on the sixteenth of June by the Julian calendar. That is the day after Vidovdan, not Vidovdan, and the distinction is worth keeping precisely because so much else in this sequence really does land on the feast. A treaty binding Serbia to Vienna is signed one day off the national day. Thirty three years later the two states will be at war, and the war will begin on the feast itself, in a town neither of them expects to matter.
suggested_refs: The Austro-Serbian Alliance of 1881, dated one day after Vidovdan

stops.name: Sarajevo, the corner by the delicatessen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinates are the assassination site, not the Latin Bridge, where the research pool had wrongly pinned it
stops.campa: Gavrilo Princip shoots the Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife on Vidovdan, at the corner where the motorcade turns off the Appel Quay and the car stalls in front of a delicatessen. He fires from the pavement, not from the Latin Bridge a few metres to the south, which is where the plaques and the photographs have put him ever since. The twenty eighth of June is the feast of Saint Vitus by the calendar the empire itself uses, and the assassin picks the day before he picks the corner.
suggested_refs: The corner of the Appel Quay at Schiller's delicatessen, Sarajevo, 28 June 1914

stops.name: Belgrade, the Vidovdan Constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the venue is a gap. The House of the National Assembly was only dedicated in 1936, with construction suspended 1920-1926, so it cannot be the place, and the pin is central Belgrade
stops.campa: King Alexander proclaims the constitution of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes on Vidovdan, and it is remembered by the day rather than by anything inside it: the Vidovdan Constitution. Where in Belgrade the proclamation happened is established by no source reached here. The National Assembly building usually named for it was not dedicated until 1936, and its construction was suspended from 1920 to 1926, so it cannot be the place. The gap is left open.
suggested_refs: The Vidovdan Constitution of 28 June 1921, named for the day rather than its content

stops.name: Gazimestan, six hundred years to the day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Six hundred years to the day after the battle, Slobodan Milosevic speaks at the monument on the field to a crowd of hundreds of thousands. It is the first open Vidovdan commemoration since the communist period. The saint whose passio has him lifted out of Rome by an angel and set down beside a river in Lucania is by now a date on which a Yugoslav politician can summon most of a nation to a hillside, and be understood by all of it without explaining anything at all.
suggested_refs: The Gazimestan speech of 28 June 1989, on the six hundredth anniversary of Kosovo

segments.name: The Scattered Body and the Feast

stops.name: San Vito Romano, Castrum Sancti Viti
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1085 by the Regesto Sublacense as cited in Italian Wikipedia; the research pool's longitude was about four kilometres west of the town and is corrected
stops.campa: East of Rome a fortified hill town appears in the Regesto Sublacense as Castrum Sancti Viti, land granted to the monastery of Subiaco. It keeps the name. Its coat of arms still shows the saint armed, palm in hand, dog at his side, the dog being one of the animals attached to him along with the rooster and the lion. No relic came here and no translation is recorded. A place took his name in the eleventh century, and nine hundred years later the name is still on the road signs.
suggested_refs: The 1085 Regesto Sublacense entry naming Castrum Sancti Viti
The arms of San Vito Romano: the saint armed, with palm and dog

stops.name: Polignano a Mare, an arm and a knee
stops.date_confidence: undated: Italian Wikipedia gives no date for the arrival of the Polignano relics, and the year here is a placeholder inside the modern cult period
stops.campa: On the Apulian coast Polignano a Mare keeps in reliquaries an arm bone and a knee patella of Saint Vitus. No source reached dates their arrival. They join a list that does not add up: an arm at Prague, a whole body at Omegna, a grave at Marigliano, a grave beside the Sele, whatever Corvey retained and whatever Pavia sent north. The saint is distributed across Europe in pieces that exceed one body, which is normal for a popular medieval cult and is recorded here as a gap rather than as a chain.
suggested_refs: The arm bone and knee patella reliquaries of Polignano a Mare

stops.name: Omegna, the urn of the adoptive patron
stops.date_confidence: undated: the source names neither a date nor a route, and the year here is a placeholder. Coordinates corrected from the research pool
stops.campa: In Piedmont, at the head of Lake Orta, the church of Sant Ambrogio at Omegna holds what it calls the urn with the body of San Vito, martyr, patron of Omegna. He is the town's adoptive patron and his festival runs over the last two Sundays of August. A whole body in the Alps, an arm in Prague, a knee in Apulia. The source names no date and no route by which a body said to have died in Lucania arrived at a lake five hundred kilometres north of the plain of the Sele.
suggested_refs: The urn of San Vito in the Chiesa di Sant'Ambrogio, Omegna

stops.name: Mazara del Vallo, the silver statue and the festino
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1614 for the co-patronage; the research pool said the statue is processed in autumn, contradicting its own neighbouring entry, and the Italian source gives late August
stops.campa: Mazara del Vallo names him co-patron beside the Santissimo Salvatore, and keeps a silver statue of him in the church of San Michele through the year. The festino, which once occupied the four days before the fifteenth of June, now falls between the second to last and the last week of August, when the statue goes out through the city that says it produced him. Sixteen centuries after the traditional birth, in the town where the passio begins, the boy comes back out into the street.
suggested_refs: The silver statue of San Vito in the Chiesa di San Michele, Mazara del Vallo

stops.name: Rome, the Holy See strikes two names
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the calendar reform
stops.campa: The reform of the General Roman Calendar removes Modestus and Crescentia. Vitus is kept, alone, on the fifteenth of June, at reduced rank. The tutor and the nurse who carried him out of his father's house, who were hung up beside him and died with him beside the river, are judged probably fictitious and struck. The old Latin mass for the day, which is still said, asks their intercession together, all three names inside one clause, as the church asked it for fourteen hundred years.
stops.quote: Grant to Thy church, O Lord, we beseech Thee, through the intercession of Thy holy Martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, not to be highminded, but to advance in that humility which is pleasing in Thy sight, that despising evil, she may practice with overflowing charity whatsoever things are right.
stops.quote_source: Missale Romanum, Collect for the Mass of Sts. Vitus, Modestus and Crescentia, 15 June
suggested_refs: The 1969 revision of the General Roman Calendar and the removal of Modestus and Crescentia

stops.name: Forio, Ischia, the basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1988 for the basilica status; the parish is older and undated in the source
stops.campa: On Ischia, on the island's high ground, Forio keeps him as town patron, and its mother church is raised to the rank of basilica in July 1988. The island sits on the sea road between Sicily and Rome that the legend's own geography implies, and no source reached supplies a landing story here to match the one San Vito Lo Capo tells. The patronage exists here without the story that usually comes with it. Any coastal town can produce a landing story on request, and Forio has not produced one, so the gap is recorded as a gap.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di San Vito at Forio, Ischia, raised to basilica in July 1988

stops.name: San Vito Lo Capo, the disembarking of the saints
stops.date_confidence: modern observance, annual; the year is a placeholder for a recurring feast
stops.campa: Every fifteenth of June the town on the cape puts three performers in a boat and lands them on the beach at sunset as Vito, Crescenzia and Modesto, then carries the statue through the streets and burns fireworks over the water. The passio is thirteen hundred years old and the historical content of it is nil. The town restages it anyway, every year, on the sand below the fortified church, and nobody standing on that beach treats the question of whether it happened as a question.
suggested_refs: Lo sbarco dei santi at San Vito Lo Capo, every 15 June
